title: Partita No. 6 in E minor
hook: The last and grandest of Bach’s keyboard partitas, opening with a toccata that holds a fugue at its heart, played on the harpsichord.

painting.title: Family Group at a Harpsichord
painting.collection: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (on loan to Rijksmuseum Twenthe, Enschede)
painting.pairingNote: A mother at the harpsichord among her family, painted eight years after the partitas were published for music lovers to play at home, and an echo of the music notebook of 1725 for Bach’s wife, Anna Magdalena, which opens with early versions of the Third and this Sixth Partita.

facts: A partita, for Bach, is a [[suite|suite]]: a chain of dances in one key, opened by a free prelude. He published his six keyboard partitas one by one from 1726, then together in 1731 as the first part of his *Clavier-Übung*, “keyboard practice”, “for music lovers, to refresh their spirits”. He called the volume his Opus 1: it was the first of his works he published himself.

The Sixth Partita is the last of the set and one of the two largest, with the Fourth. An early version of it stands near the beginning of the music notebook he began for his wife, Anna Magdalena, in 1725, just after the Third Partita.

It opens with a [[toccata|toccata]], a “touch piece” meant to show off the player. Bach’s is weighty rather than brilliant: a free opening, a long three-voice [[fugue|fugue]], and the opening again. Then come the dances: [[allemande|allemande]], [[courante|courante]] (here *Corrente*), a short Air, [[sarabande|sarabande]], a [[gavotte|gavotte]]-like *Tempo di Gavotta* and a [[gigue|gigue]] written as a fugue.

This recording uses the harpsichord, one of the keyboard instruments Bach wrote for. It has no [[sustain-pedal|sustain pedal]] and cannot play louder or softer by touch: the player shapes the music by choosing between its two keyboards and their sets of strings, by spreading chords, by ornaments and by timing.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a toccata with a fugue inside it (I), two richly ornamented dances (II–III), a lively interlude (IV), the slow heart of the work (V), a quick gavotte, and a jig in fugue whose theme turns upside down halfway (VI–VII).

movements.heading: Toccata
movements.summary: The longest movement and the gateway to the partita. A free, declamatory opening, full of runs and full chords; then a long, grave fugue in three voices; then the opening music returns to close the frame.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: rolling chords and sweeping runs over a slow bass, like an improvisation.

mainIdeas.name: The sigh
mainIdeas.description: a three-note figure, a clashing note that falls to rest, first heard in the opening and then built into the fugue’s theme.

mainIdeas.name: The fugue theme
mainIdeas.description: slow, serious, beginning with that sigh.

stops.hear: Full, spread chords and running figures that sweep across both hands
stops.happening: The free opening of the toccata

stops.hear: The runs settle into a pattern, with a falling, sighing figure repeated
stops.happening: The sigh motif that will feed the fugue

stops.hear: A single line begins a solemn theme; a second voice enters, then a third
The theme passes through new keys; the texture thickens and the sighs multiply
stops.happening: The fugue’s middle and its long final build

stops.hear: The free chords and runs of the beginning come back
stops.happening: The opening returns to frame the fugue

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A broad, spread final chord

notice: Listen for how the harpsichord makes a big sound without a pedal: chords are spread from the bottom note upwards, and quick notes fill the space between them, so the instrument keeps ringing.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Igor Kipnis (1930–2002), son of the bass Alexander Kipnis, was one of the best-known American harpsichordists. His two albums of the six partitas first appeared in 1977, when the magazine *High Fidelity* called the playing “glitteringly bright” and “robustly sonorous”; they were reissued on CD in 2000, which is the edition on Spotify. On this album the Sixth Partita is tracks 15–21, after the Third and Fifth. A reviewer of the reissue singled out this Toccata as among the finest on record.

movements.heading: Allemanda
movements.summary: A moderate dance in four, slow and stately here, covered in ornaments. Two halves, each played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The line
mainIdeas.description: a flowing melody wound round with [[trill|trill]]s and turns, over a steady bass.

stops.hear: A stately, flowing melody, decorated with quick ornaments
The opening again
The melody sets off from a new note and moves through other keys
The second half again

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: The line comes to rest on a low E

notice: On a harpsichord an ornament is also a way of making a note seem louder: a trill keeps a long note sounding. Listen for the trills on the most important notes.

movements.heading: Corrente
movements.summary: A fast dance in three, in the Italian style, full of quick runs and syncopations that pull against the beat.

mainIdeas.name: The runs
mainIdeas.description: quick, light scales in the right hand.

mainIdeas.name: The syncopation
mainIdeas.description: notes that land just off the beat, making the rhythm limp and leap.

stops.hear: Quick runs over a bass that keeps catching the beat a moment late
stops.happening: The first half of the [[courante|courante]], with [[syncopation|syncopation]]

stops.hear: The opening again
The runs turn to new keys; the off-beat accents grow stronger
The second half again

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A firm close on E

notice: Try tapping the beat. Every few bars the music seems to slip off it, then lands back on it.

movements.heading: Air
movements.summary: A short, quick interlude between the dances, almost all in running notes. “Air” here simply means a tune, not a slow song.

mainIdeas.name: The running line
mainIdeas.description: a busy, chattering melody over a walking bass.

stops.hear: A brisk, chattering line
The opening again
The line runs on, longer, through other keys
The second half again

stops.label: Last 5 seconds
stops.hear: A quick close

notice: This is the lightest moment in the partita, placed just before the slowest. Listen to how it clears the air.

movements.heading: Sarabande
movements.summary: The slow heart of the partita, and one of the most intense sarabandes Bach wrote. The melody is so densely ornamented that the ornaments become the music: broken chords, turns and trills carry the feeling.

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: slow, searching, constantly decorated, over chords that lean on the second beat.

mainIdeas.name: The harmony
mainIdeas.description: unexpected, aching chords that pull the music away from home.

stops.hear: A slow, richly decorated melody over spread chords
The opening again, the ornaments slightly changed
A longer second half, moving through darker keys
The second half again

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A slow, spread final chord

notice: Listen to the chords: on the harpsichord they are often broken, played from bottom to top, so that each one blooms rather than strikes. That is how the player makes a soft, sustained sound on an instrument that cannot sustain.

movements.heading: Tempo di Gavotta
movements.summary: “In the tempo of a gavotte”: a quick dance in two, its rhythm bouncing between dotted notes and groups of three.

mainIdeas.name: The bounce
mainIdeas.description: a skipping rhythm, with quick notes in threes against a steady two-beat bass.

stops.hear: A quick, skipping tune in two
The opening again
The skipping tune moves through other keys
The second half again

stops.label: Last 5 seconds
stops.hear: A neat close

notice: Notice the triplets: three quick notes in the space of two, which make the dance feel light and slightly uneven.

movements.heading: Gigue
movements.summary: The finale is a jig written as a [[fugue|fugue]]: an angular, jagged theme enters in three voices. In the second half Bach turns the theme upside down, so that where it rose it now falls, and builds a second fugue from it.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: angular, with sharp dotted rhythms and wide leaps, clashing with the line set against it.

stops.hear: A jagged theme alone, then a second voice, then a third
stops.happening: The first half: a fugue on the [[gigue|gigue]] theme

stops.hear: The opening again
The theme returns upside down, falling where it had risen
stops.happening: The second half, on the inverted theme

stops.hear: The second half again

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: All three voices drive to a firm close on E

notice: Sing or hum the first few notes of the theme at the start, then listen for its mirror image at the start of the second half. It is the same shape, turned upside down.

threads.title: The sigh
threads.body: The three-note falling figure heard in the Toccata’s opening launches the theme of its fugue and comes back again and again as the fugue drives to its end. Listen for falling, sighing steps in the slow dances too.

threads.title: Fugue as frame
threads.body: The partita begins and ends with fugues: one inside the Toccata, one disguised as a jig. Between them stand the dances.

threads.title: The harpsichord’s art
threads.body: No pedal and no touch dynamics: everything the listener hears as loud, soft, sustained or singing comes from registration, spread chords, ornaments and timing.
